Unfortunately, large amounts of ELISA data are published without confirming the accuracy of the individual assay system. Consequently, assay results containing BG noise reaction values are considered true antibody-antigen reaction values, as described later. Furthermore, it is not well recognized that approximately 20–50% of the OD values obtained using BSA-Tween and BSA-Triton-X 100 buffer systems are attributed to the non-specific protein-protein interactions between immunoglobulins and antigen molecules [3]. Therefore, it is critical to confirm the accuracy and reliability of individual assay systems with an inhibition test. The following is an appropriate protocol to perform an inhibition test.1)Dissolve the antigen at 400 μg/ml in an appropriate Blocking/Sample Dilution Buffer, then serially dilute to make 200, 100, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.3, and 0 μg/ml solutions.2)Prepare 2× concentration of antibody solution in the same buffer.3)Mix equal volumes of antigen and antibody solutions, and incubate at room temperature for 2 h or at 4 °C overnight.4)Add 100 μl of the mixed solution to both antigen non-coated and antigen-coated wells, and run the assay to determine the antigen-specific inhibition.5)Calculate the corrected OD values by subtracting the BG OD values in antigen non-coated wells from the OD values in antigen-coated wells. Then, calculate the inhibition percentage by comparing the OD values in wells containing inhibition antigen with OD values in the control wells without inhibition antigen (see Fig. 8, Fig. 10).

Antibody assay results vary significantly depending on the buffer system used, because different buffer components contribute to different non-specific reactions. To demonstrate the importance of eliminating all types of non-specific reactions, human serum IgG anti-E. coli and anti-CCP antibodies were assayed in different buffer systems under the same conditions.

steps.title: Prepare antigen dilution series
steps.instruction: Dissolve the antigen at 400 µg ml⁻¹ in the chosen Blocking/Sample Dilution Buffer, then perform serial 2‑fold dilutions to obtain antigen concentrations of 200, 100, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.3 and 0 µg ml⁻¹.

steps.title: Prepare 2× antibody solution
steps.instruction: Dilute the specific antibody in the same Blocking/Sample Dilution Buffer to a final concentration that is twice the intended assay concentration (2×).

steps.title: Incubate antigen‑antibody mixture
steps.instruction: Mix equal volumes of each antigen dilution (from step 1) with the 2× antibody solution (step 2). Incubate the mixture at room temperature for 2 h **or** at 4 °C overnight.

steps.title: Add mixture to ELISA wells
steps.instruction: Dispense 100 µl of each antigen‑antibody mixture into both antigen‑coated wells and antigen‑non‑coated (blank) wells of a micro‑titer plate. Run the ELISA as usual to measure OD values for inhibition assessment.

steps.title: Stabilize unstable antigens (if needed)
steps.instruction: If the antigen is unstable in solution, dissolve it at 5–10 mg ml⁻¹ in 5 % sucrose, aliquot 0.1 ml portions, lyophilize, and store at –20 °C. For coating, dilute the lyophilized antigen 1:100 with coating buffer.

steps.title: Prepare standard antibody stock
steps.instruction: Select an appropriate antibody (monoclonal, polyclonal or positive serum) and determine its titer. Dilute the antibody to 320 units ml⁻¹ in 4 % BSA dissolved in 0.02 M Tris‑0.15 M NaCl buffer (pH 7.2) containing 5 % sucrose. Aliquot 0.1 ml, lyophilize, and store at –20 °C. Reconstitute each vial with 1 ml Blocking/Sample Dilution Buffer to obtain a working standard of 32 units ml⁻¹.

steps.title: Prepare secondary antibody solution
steps.instruction: Dilute the HRP‑conjugated secondary antibody in 50 % ethylene glycol containing 1 % BSA. If the final assay dilution will be 1/1000 or 1/2000, prepare a 1/5 or 1/10 intermediate stock in the same EG‑BSA solution, aliquot 50 µl per vial, and store at –20 °C. Immediately before use, dissolve one vial in 10 ml secondary‑antibody dilution buffer. **Do not** use glycerol, as it can inactivate the peroxidase.

steps.title: Prepare washing buffer
steps.instruction: Make a 20× PBS‑1 % Tween 20 stock solution and keep it at room temperature. Just before each assay, dilute the stock 20‑fold with endotoxin‑free distilled water to obtain 1× wash buffer.

steps.title: Map ELISA plate layout
steps.instruction: Design the plate to include (1) Blank (BL) wells, (2) Background (BG) wells (antigen‑non‑coated) for each sample, and (3) Antigen‑antibody wells. If sample dilution is >1/1000, BG wells may be omitted when using ChonBlock™; if dilution is <1/500, include BG wells for each sample.

steps.title: Block plate and add samples
steps.instruction: Block the plate with ChonBlock™ (or the chosen blocking buffer) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Dilute each serum or sample in ChonBlock™ (or the selected buffer) at the appropriate dilution (e.g., 1/200 for RA serum comparisons). Add diluted samples to the mapped wells (antigen‑coated, BG, and BL).

steps.title: Incubate, wash, and develop ELISA
steps.instruction: Incubate the plate for the recommended time (as per the specific assay) at room temperature. Wash wells with freshly prepared 1× wash buffer (typically 3–5 washes). Add the secondary antibody solution prepared in step 6, incubate as required, wash again, and add the appropriate substrate for HRP detection. Measure absorbance (OD) at the specified wavelength.

steps.title: Calculate antibody titers
steps.instruction: 1) Average duplicate OD values for BL, standards, and test samples. 2) Subtract the averaged BL OD from all other averaged ODs. 3) If BG values were measured, subtract the BG OD (from non‑coated wells) from the antigen‑coated well OD for each sample. 4) Plot corrected OD of standards versus known units ml⁻¹ on a log‑log graph and fit a regression line. 5) Use the regression to determine the concentration (units ml⁻¹) of each test sample. 6) For inhibition assays, calculate inhibition % = [1 – (OD with inhibition antigen / OD control)] × 100.

steps.title: Store reagents appropriately
steps.instruction: Aliquot all prepared reagents (antigen solutions, standards, secondary antibody stocks, wash buffer stock) into multiple vials and store at 4 °C or –20 °C as indicated to minimize batch‑to‑batch variation.

description: It is critical to reduce or eliminate non-specific reactions in any immunological assay system to avoid false positive and negative results. It is especially important to consider BG noise reaction caused by the hydrophobic binding of immunoglobulins in sample specimens to solid surfaces in indirect ELISA systems for assaying serum antibodies, particularly at low sample serum dilutions. In addition, non-specific binding of immunoglobulins to antigenic molecules by protein-protein interactions also creates unpredictable degrees of false positive reactions. We encourage all ELISA users to take into consideration the various types of non-specific reactions involved in the indirect ELISA system, and use appropriate buffer systems and proper ELISA design to prevent further misuse of the ELISA technique and misinterpretation of serological antibody assay data.
